set_title: Aortic regurgitation peripheral signs: de Musset sign, Quincke sign, Duroziez sign, Traube sign, Muller sign and Hill sign
stem: A 52-year-old man has a blood pressure of 170/45 mm Hg and a bounding pulse. When the examiner lightly presses a fingernail tip, the nail bed alternately flushes and blanches with each heartbeat.
oneliner: 52M, BP 170/45 + nail bed flushes and blanches with each beat → ?

whyNot.A: de Musset sign is head bobbing; his finding is **nail bed flushing and blanching**
whyNot.B: Duroziez sign is a femoral bruit on compression; his finding is the **nail bed**
whyNot.C: Traube sign is a femoral pistol-shot sound; his finding is **nail bed pulsation**
whyNot.D: Hill sign compares popliteal and brachial pressures; here **nail bed pulsates** with each beat

why: Quincke sign is visible capillary pulsation in the nail bed caused by a wide pulse pressure. The **nail bed flushing and blanching with each beat** points to aortic regurgitation.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Popliteal systolic BP far above brachial

idea.rule: Pulsating nail bed capillaries = Quincke sign of aortic regurgitation.
also: Wide pulse pressure from low diastolic pressure

set_title: Aortic regurgitation peripheral signs: de Musset sign, Quincke sign, Duroziez sign, Traube sign, Muller sign and Hill sign
stem: A 27-year-old tall man with long arms and a pectus excavatum has a head that nods in time with each heartbeat. Blood pressure is 160/40 mm Hg.
oneliner: 27M, tall with long arms + head nods with each heartbeat, BP 160/40 → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Mitral stenosis gives a diastolic rumble, not **wide pulse pressure 160/40** and head bobbing
whyNot.C: Outflow obstruction does not widen pulse pressure like his **BP 160/40**
whyNot.D: Prolapse gives a click and late systolic murmur, not **BP 160/40 with head bobbing**
whyNot.E: Aortic stenosis narrows pulse pressure; he has **BP 160/40**

why: De Musset sign is head bobbing with each pulse from a large stroke volume and rapid diastolic runoff. **Wide pulse pressure** in a Marfan-like patient points to aortic regurgitation.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Popliteal systolic BP far above brachial

idea.rule: Head bobbing with wide pulse pressure = aortic regurgitation.
also: Marfan aortic root dilation is a classic cause

set_title: Aortic regurgitation peripheral signs: de Musset sign, Quincke sign, Duroziez sign, Traube sign, Muller sign and Hill sign
stem: A 60-year-old man has a bounding pulse and BP 175/40 mm Hg. When a stethoscope is pressed firmly over his femoral artery, a bruit is heard in both systole and diastole.
oneliner: 60M, BP 175/40 + femoral bruit in systole and diastole on compression → ?

whyNot.A: de Musset sign is head bobbing; his finding is a **femoral bruit on compression**
whyNot.B: Quincke sign is nail bed pulsation; his finding is a **femoral bruit**
whyNot.D: Traube sign is a pistol-shot sound without compression; his bruit needs **firm pressure**
whyNot.E: Muller sign is uvular pulsation; his finding is a **femoral to-and-fro bruit**

why: Duroziez sign is a to-and-fro femoral bruit produced by compressing the artery. The **systolic and diastolic bruit** reflects forward flow plus diastolic reversal of aortic regurgitation.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Popliteal systolic BP far above brachial

idea.rule: Femoral bruit in systole and diastole on compression = Duroziez sign.

set_title: Aortic regurgitation peripheral signs: de Musset sign, Quincke sign, Duroziez sign, Traube sign, Muller sign and Hill sign
stem: A 45-year-old man has a bounding pulse. Brachial blood pressure is 150/40 mm Hg and popliteal systolic pressure is 220 mm Hg.
oneliner: 45M, bounding pulse + popliteal systolic 70 mm Hg above brachial → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Mild disease gives a small gap, not **70 mm Hg higher popliteal pressure**
whyNot.B: Coarctation lowers leg pressure; his **popliteal pressure is 70 mm Hg higher**
whyNot.C: Aortic stenosis narrows pulse pressure; he has **BP 150/40**
whyNot.E: Mitral regurgitation does not widen pulse pressure; his **diastolic pressure is 40**

why: Hill sign is popliteal systolic pressure exceeding brachial by more than 60 mm Hg, seen in aortic regurgitation. A **70 mm Hg gap** indicates severe disease.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Popliteal systolic BP far above brachial

idea.rule: Popliteal minus brachial systolic over 60 mm Hg = severe aortic regurgitation.

set_title: Endocarditis skin and eye signs: Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, Splinter hemorrhages and Conjunctival petechiae
stem: A 34-year-old man who injects heroin has had 5 days of fever and a new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. His soles have flat, painless red macules.
oneliner: 34M, IV drug use, fever, new murmur + flat painless red macules on soles → ?

whyNot.A: Osler nodes are tender and raised; his lesions are **flat and painless**
whyNot.C: Roth spots are retinal hemorrhages; his lesions are **macules on the soles**
whyNot.D: Splinter hemorrhages are linear streaks under nails; his are **macules on the soles**
whyNot.E: Conjunctival petechiae are on the eyelid lining; his lesions are **on the soles**

why: Janeway lesions are painless flat red macules on palms and soles from septic microemboli. **Painless soles lesions with fever and a new murmur** suggest infective endocarditis.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Painless red macules on palms, soles
Painful raised nodules on finger pads
Thin dark red lines under nails
Pinpoint hemorrhages on the palpebral conjunctiva

idea.rule: Painless flat palm or sole macules = Janeway lesions, from septic emboli.
also: Osler nodes are tender and raised instead

set_title: Endocarditis skin and eye signs: Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, Splinter hemorrhages and Conjunctival petechiae
stem: A 68-year-old woman with a prosthetic aortic valve has had 2 weeks of fever. She has tender, raised, pea-sized nodules on the pads of several fingers.
oneliner: 68F, prosthetic valve, fever + tender raised nodules on finger pads → ?

whyNot.A: Janeway lesions are painless and flat; hers are **tender, raised nodules**
whyNot.B: Roth spots are retinal hemorrhages; hers are **nodules on finger pads**
whyNot.C: Splinter hemorrhages are thin streaks under nails; hers are **raised nodules on finger pads**
whyNot.D: Conjunctival petechiae are flat eyelid-lining dots; hers are **tender finger-pad nodules**

why: Osler nodes are painful, raised nodules on fingertip pads, thought to arise from immune complex deposition. **Tender finger-pad nodules with fever and a prosthetic valve** suggest infective endocarditis.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Painless red macules on palms, soles
Painful raised nodules on finger pads
Thin dark red lines under nails
Pinpoint hemorrhages on the palpebral conjunctiva

idea.rule: Tender raised finger-pad nodules = Osler nodes, immune complex phenomenon.
also: Painless flat lesions are Janeway lesions

set_title: Endocarditis skin and eye signs: Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, Splinter hemorrhages and Conjunctival petechiae
stem: A 41-year-old man has had fever for 2 weeks and has a new murmur. Funduscopy shows retinal hemorrhages with pale white centers.
oneliner: 41M, fever, new murmur + retinal hemorrhages with pale centers → ?
ask: Which process best explains this finding?

options.A: Immune complex injury to small vessels
options.C: Thrombus in the central retinal vein

whyNot.B: Hypertensive retinopathy shows flame hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots; he has **fever**
whyNot.C: Vein occlusion gives diffuse hemorrhages; his have **pale centers with fever**
whyNot.D: Cytomegalovirus retinitis needs profound immunosuppression; he has **fever and a new murmur**
whyNot.E: Diabetic neovascularization has no link to **fever and a new murmur**

answer: Immune complex injury to small vessels
why: Roth spots are retinal hemorrhages with pale centers attributed to immune complex vessel injury. **Fever with a new murmur** makes infective endocarditis the setting.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Painless red macules on palms, soles
Painful raised nodules on finger pads
Thin dark red lines under nails
Pinpoint hemorrhages on the palpebral conjunctiva

idea.rule: Pale-centered retinal hemorrhage with fever and murmur = endocarditis Roth spots.
also: Immune complex phenomenon, like Osler nodes

set_title: Endocarditis skin and eye signs: Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, Splinter hemorrhages and Conjunctival petechiae
stem: A 55-year-old man has had fever for 3 weeks and a new regurgitant murmur at the apex. Several fingernails show thin, dark red linear streaks.
oneliner: 55M, 3 weeks of fever, new apical murmur + dark linear streaks under nails → ?
ask: Which condition best explains these findings?

whyNot.A: Rheumatic fever causes migratory arthritis, not **nail streaks after 3 weeks of fever**
whyNot.B: Dilated cardiomyopathy does not cause **fever or subungual streaks**
whyNot.D: Pericarditis gives a friction rub, not a **new regurgitant murmur with nail streaks**
whyNot.E: Papillary rupture is acute after an infarct; he has **3 weeks of fever**

why: Splinter hemorrhages are thin subungual streaks from microemboli. **Fever plus a new regurgitant murmur and nail streaks** is infective endocarditis.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Painless red macules on palms, soles
Painful raised nodules on finger pads
Thin dark red lines under nails
Pinpoint hemorrhages on the palpebral conjunctiva

idea.rule: Fever, new regurgitant murmur and subungual streaks = infective endocarditis.
also: Also seen in trauma and vasculitis

set_title: Named murmurs: Austin Flint murmur, Graham Steell murmur, Carey Coombs murmur, Gallavardin phenomenon, Still murmur and Gibson (machinery) murmur
stem: A 62-year-old man has BP 180/40 mm Hg and an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border. A low-pitched mid-to-late diastolic rumble is heard at the apex. Echocardiography shows a normal mitral valve.
oneliner: 62M, BP 180/40, early diastolic murmur + apical diastolic rumble, normal mitral valve → ?

whyNot.A: Graham Steell is pulmonic regurgitation; he has **wide pulse pressure** and an apical rumble
whyNot.B: Carey Coombs murmur is seen in rheumatic fever; his **mitral valve is normal**
whyNot.C: Gallavardin phenomenon is a systolic murmur at the apex; his rumble is **diastolic**
whyNot.D: Still murmur is an innocent systolic murmur of children; his is **diastolic**

why: Austin Flint murmur is an apical mid-diastolic rumble in severe aortic regurgitation, from the regurgitant jet impinging on the anterior mitral leaflet. The **normal mitral valve** excludes mitral stenosis.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Mid-diastolic apical rumble without mitral stenosis
Early diastolic decrescendo, left upper sternal border
AS murmur sounds musical at apex, mimics MR
Musical vibratory systolic murmur in a child

idea.rule: Apical diastolic rumble with aortic regurgitation and normal mitral valve = Austin Flint.
also: Mitral stenosis has an opening snap

set_title: Named murmurs: Austin Flint murmur, Graham Steell murmur, Carey Coombs murmur, Gallavardin phenomenon, Still murmur and Gibson (machinery) murmur
stem: A 38-year-old woman with long-standing mitral stenosis develops severe pulmonary hypertension. A high-pitched blowing early diastolic decrescendo murmur is now heard at the left upper sternal border and increases with inspiration.
oneliner: 38F, mitral stenosis, pulmonary hypertension + early diastolic murmur at left upper sternal border → ?

whyNot.B: Austin Flint is an apical rumble; this is at the **left upper sternal border**
whyNot.C: Carey Coombs is soft and apical mid-diastolic; hers is **early diastolic with pulmonary hypertension**
whyNot.D: Gibson murmur is continuous in patent ductus; hers is **early diastolic only**
whyNot.E: Still murmur is an innocent systolic murmur; hers is **diastolic with pulmonary hypertension**

why: Graham Steell murmur is the early diastolic murmur of pulmonic regurgitation caused by pulmonary hypertension. **Mitral stenosis with severe pulmonary hypertension** is the classic setting.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Mid-diastolic apical rumble without mitral stenosis
Early diastolic decrescendo, left upper sternal border
AS murmur sounds musical at apex, mimics MR
Musical vibratory systolic murmur in a child

idea.rule: Early diastolic murmur at left upper sternal border with pulmonary hypertension = Graham Steell.

set_title: Named murmurs: Austin Flint murmur, Graham Steell murmur, Carey Coombs murmur, Gallavardin phenomenon, Still murmur and Gibson (machinery) murmur
stem: A 2-year-old boy born at 28 weeks has a continuous machine-like murmur heard below the left clavicle. His pulses are bounding and his pulse pressure is wide.
oneliner: 2M, born at 28 weeks + continuous machine-like murmur below left clavicle → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: A ventricular septal defect gives a holosystolic murmur, not a **continuous machine-like murmur**
whyNot.B: Coarctation causes upper-limb hypertension; this boy has a **continuous murmur and bounding pulses**
whyNot.D: Tetralogy causes cyanosis with a systolic murmur; this murmur is **continuous with bounding pulses**
whyNot.E: A secundum defect gives fixed split S2, not a **continuous murmur**

why: A continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle is the Gibson murmur of patent ductus arteriosus. **Prematurity with bounding pulses** raises the risk of a persistent duct.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Mid-diastolic apical rumble without mitral stenosis
Early diastolic decrescendo, left upper sternal border
AS murmur sounds musical at apex, mimics MR
Musical vibratory systolic murmur in a child

idea.rule: Continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle = patent ductus arteriosus.
also: Prostaglandin E1 keeps the duct open

set_title: Named murmurs: Austin Flint murmur, Graham Steell murmur, Carey Coombs murmur, Gallavardin phenomenon, Still murmur and Gibson (machinery) murmur
stem: A healthy 5-year-old girl has a soft, musical, vibratory systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. It is loudest when supine and softens on standing. Growth, pulses and the rest of the examination are normal.
oneliner: 5F, healthy + soft musical systolic murmur, softer on standing → ?

whyNot.A: A small VSD gives a harsh holosystolic murmur, not a **soft musical murmur**
whyNot.B: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy gets louder on standing; this murmur **softens on standing**
whyNot.C: Pulmonic stenosis gives an ejection click and harsh murmur, not a **soft musical** one
whyNot.E: A bicuspid valve gives an ejection click, not a **vibratory murmur softer on standing**

why: Still murmur is a benign, vibratory flow murmur of healthy children. A **soft musical murmur that softens on standing** with normal growth needs no workup.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Mid-diastolic apical rumble without mitral stenosis
Early diastolic decrescendo, left upper sternal border
AS murmur sounds musical at apex, mimics MR
Musical vibratory systolic murmur in a child

idea.rule: Soft musical systolic murmur that fades on standing in a healthy child = innocent.

set_title: Pericardial signs: Beck triad, Kussmaul sign, Ewart sign, Pericardial knock and Electrical alternans
stem: A 24-year-old man is brought in after a stab wound to the left chest. His blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg, his neck veins are distended and his heart sounds are faint.
oneliner: 24M, stab wound to chest + BP 80/50, distended neck veins, faint heart sounds → ?

whyNot.A: Kussmaul sign is a JVP rise on inspiration; he has **hypotension and faint sounds**
whyNot.C: Ewart sign is dullness below the left scapula, not **hypotension and faint sounds**
whyNot.D: Pericardial knock is an extra diastolic sound; he has **hypotension and faint sounds**
whyNot.E: Electrical alternans is an ECG finding; this is the **hypotension, veins and sounds** combination

why: Beck triad is hypotension, jugular venous distension and muffled heart sounds, the classic findings of cardiac tamponade. **Penetrating chest trauma** is a typical cause.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds
Dullness, bronchial breathing below left scapula
QRS height alternates beat to beat

idea.rule: Hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds = Beck triad of tamponade.

set_title: Pericardial signs: Beck triad, Kussmaul sign, Ewart sign, Pericardial knock and Electrical alternans
stem: A 58-year-old man with prior mediastinal radiation has ascites and leg edema. His jugular venous pressure rises when he inspires.
oneliner: 58M, prior chest radiation, ascites, edema + JVP rises on inspiration → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Tamponade presents acutely with hypotension, not **months of ascites and edema**
whyNot.B: Left-sided failure causes pulmonary congestion; his **JVP rises on inspiration with ascites**
whyNot.C: SVC obstruction causes facial swelling, not **ascites and a paradoxical JVP rise**
whyNot.E: Mitral regurgitation does not cause **a JVP rise on inspiration or ascites**

why: Kussmaul sign is a paradoxical rise in jugular venous pressure on inspiration because a rigid pericardium blocks right heart filling. **Prior radiation with ascites and edema** fits constrictive pericarditis.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds
Dullness, bronchial breathing below left scapula
QRS height alternates beat to beat

idea.rule: JVP rising on inspiration = Kussmaul sign, classically constrictive pericarditis.
also: Restrictive cardiomyopathy can also cause it

set_title: Pericardial signs: Beck triad, Kussmaul sign, Ewart sign, Pericardial knock and Electrical alternans
stem: A 56-year-old man with tuberculosis years ago now has dyspnea, ankle edema and ascites. A high-pitched extra sound is heard early in diastole shortly after S2. Chest x-ray shows a calcified rim around the heart.
oneliner: 56M, prior TB, edema, ascites + early diastolic extra sound after S2, calcified rim around heart → ?

whyNot.A: Beck triad is acute tamponade; he has **chronic edema and a calcified pericardium**
whyNot.B: Kussmaul sign is a JVP rise on inspiration, not an **extra sound after S2**
whyNot.D: Ewart sign is lung dullness below the left scapula, not an **early diastolic sound**
whyNot.E: Electrical alternans is an ECG finding, not an **extra sound after S2**

why: Pericardial knock is a high-pitched early diastolic sound as a rigid pericardium abruptly stops ventricular filling. **Calcified pericardium after tuberculosis** points to constrictive pericarditis.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds
Dullness, bronchial breathing below left scapula
QRS height alternates beat to beat

idea.rule: Early diastolic knock after S2 with calcified pericardium = constrictive pericarditis.

set_title: Pericardial signs: Beck triad, Kussmaul sign, Ewart sign, Pericardial knock and Electrical alternans
stem: A 60-year-old woman on dialysis has dyspnea. Her blood pressure is 85/60 mm Hg, her neck veins are distended and an ECG shows low-voltage QRS complexes alternating in height beat to beat.
oneliner: 60F, dialysis, dyspnea, BP 85/60 + QRS height alternates beat to beat → ?
ask: What is happening in this patient?

options.A: Pulmonary embolism with right heart strain
options.E: Heart swinging in a large effusion

whyNot.A: Pulmonary embolism does not produce **alternating, low-voltage QRS complexes**
whyNot.B: Hyperkalemia causes peaked T waves, not **QRS height alternating with low voltage**
whyNot.C: Left ventricular failure does not give **low voltage with alternating QRS height**
whyNot.D: A ventricular aneurysm gives persistent ST elevation, not **QRS alternation**

answer: Heart swinging in a large effusion
why: Electrical alternans is beat-to-beat QRS amplitude variation as the heart swings within a large pericardial effusion. **Hypotension with distended neck veins** signals tamponade, here likely uremic.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds
Dullness, bronchial breathing below left scapula
QRS height alternates beat to beat

idea.rule: QRS height alternating beat to beat = swinging heart in a large effusion.
also: Uremia is a common cause in dialysis patients

set_title: Jugular venous waveform signs: Cannon a waves, Giant v waves, Absent a waves, Steep y descent and Hepatojugular reflux
stem: A 70-year-old woman has dizziness and a pulse of 38/min. Her ECG shows P waves at 80/min unrelated to the QRS complexes. Intermittent large pulsations are visible in her neck.
oneliner: 70F, pulse 38, ECG P waves unrelated to QRS + intermittent large neck pulsations → ?

whyNot.B: Giant v waves are systolic waves; hers appear with **P waves unrelated to QRS**
whyNot.C: Absent a waves occur in atrial fibrillation; she has **regular P waves at 80/min**
whyNot.D: Steep y descent is seen in constrictive pericarditis; she has **AV dissociation**
whyNot.E: Hepatojugular reflux needs abdominal pressure; hers are **intermittent pulsations with dissociated P waves**

why: Cannon a waves are giant jugular waves when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve. **P waves unrelated to the QRS** indicate AV dissociation, as in complete heart block.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve
AV dissociation, complete heart block, VT
Large systolic v waves in neck veins
Rapid early diastolic fall in JVP

idea.rule: Intermittent huge neck pulsations with AV dissociation = cannon a waves.
also: Regular cannon waves occur in junctional rhythm

set_title: Jugular venous waveform signs: Cannon a waves, Giant v waves, Absent a waves, Steep y descent and Hepatojugular reflux
stem: A 32-year-old man who injects drugs has fever, large systolic pulsations in his neck veins and a pulsatile liver edge.
oneliner: 32M, IV drug use, fever + large systolic neck vein pulsations, pulsatile liver → ?
ask: Which valve lesion best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Mitral stenosis does not cause **systolic neck pulsations or a pulsatile liver**
whyNot.C: Aortic regurgitation causes a wide pulse pressure, not a **pulsatile liver edge**
whyNot.D: Pulmonic stenosis causes a prominent a wave, not **systolic v waves**
whyNot.E: Tricuspid stenosis gives giant a waves, not **large systolic waves with a pulsatile liver**

why: Giant v waves are systolic jugular pulsations from regurgitant flow into the right atrium. A **pulsatile liver and injection drug use** point to tricuspid regurgitation, often from endocarditis.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve
AV dissociation, complete heart block, VT
Large systolic v waves in neck veins
Rapid early diastolic fall in JVP

idea.rule: Large systolic neck waves with pulsatile liver = tricuspid regurgitation.
also: Drug use makes tricuspid endocarditis likely

set_title: Jugular venous waveform signs: Cannon a waves, Giant v waves, Absent a waves, Steep y descent and Hepatojugular reflux
stem: A 76-year-old man has palpitations. His pulse is irregularly irregular at 130/min. Inspection of his neck veins shows no presystolic pulsation.
oneliner: 76M, palpitations, irregularly irregular pulse + no presystolic neck pulsation → ?

whyNot.B: Cannon a waves are large presystolic pulsations; he has **no presystolic wave**
whyNot.C: Giant v waves are large systolic waves; he has **no presystolic pulsation**
whyNot.D: Steep y descent is seen in constrictive pericarditis; he has an **irregularly irregular pulse**
whyNot.E: Hepatojugular reflux needs liver compression; he has **no presystolic wave**

why: Absent a waves occur in atrial fibrillation because the atria no longer contract in an organized way. An **irregularly irregular pulse** with no presystolic wave confirms the sign.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve
AV dissociation, complete heart block, VT
Large systolic v waves in neck veins
Rapid early diastolic fall in JVP

idea.rule: No presystolic jugular wave with irregularly irregular pulse = atrial fibrillation.
also: Atria quiver, so no atrial contraction

set_title: Jugular venous waveform signs: Cannon a waves, Giant v waves, Absent a waves, Steep y descent and Hepatojugular reflux
stem: A 66-year-old man has leg edema and orthopnea. Firm pressure over his liver for 10 seconds keeps his jugular veins elevated.
oneliner: 66M, leg edema, orthopnea + liver pressure keeps neck veins elevated → ?

whyNot.A: Hypovolemia lowers venous pressure; his **neck veins stay elevated**
whyNot.B: SVC obstruction causes facial swelling, not **leg edema and orthopnea**
whyNot.C: Cirrhosis does not raise the JVP; he has **orthopnea and leg edema**
whyNot.E: Budd-Chiari gives ascites with a normal JVP; **orthopnea** points to the heart

why: Hepatojugular reflux is a sustained rise in JVP after abdominal compression, showing the right heart cannot accept the extra venous return. **Edema and orthopnea** fit right heart failure.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve
AV dissociation, complete heart block, VT
Large systolic v waves in neck veins
Rapid early diastolic fall in JVP

idea.rule: Sustained JVP rise on liver compression = right heart failure.

set_title: Lipid and coronary clues: Levine sign, Frank sign, Tendon xanthomas, Xanthelasma and Corneal arcus
stem: A 59-year-old man describes crushing substernal pressure for 40 minutes. While answering questions, he holds a clenched fist against his sternum.
oneliner: 59M, crushing chest pressure + clenched fist held against sternum → ?

whyNot.A: Frank sign is an earlobe crease; his clue is the **clenched fist**
whyNot.B: Tendon xanthomas are tendon nodules; his clue is the **fist on his chest**
whyNot.C: Xanthelasma is a yellow eyelid plaque; his clue is the **fist on his sternum**
whyNot.D: Corneal arcus is a corneal ring; his clue is the **fist on his chest**

why: Levine sign is a clenched fist held over the sternum when describing ischemic chest pain. The **fist over the sternum with crushing pressure** points to angina or myocardial infarction.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Clenched fist held over the chest
Firm nodules on Achilles or knuckle tendons
Hypercholesterolemia if young; normal if old

idea.rule: Clenched fist over the chest describing pain = Levine sign of ischemia.
also: Not reliable alone for diagnosing MI

set_title: Lipid and coronary clues: Levine sign, Frank sign, Tendon xanthomas, Xanthelasma and Corneal arcus
stem: A 25-year-old man has firm nodules on his Achilles tendons and knuckle extensor tendons. His LDL cholesterol is 300 mg/dL and his father had a myocardial infarction at age 42.
oneliner: 25M, Achilles tendon nodules, LDL 300, father had MI at 42 → ?
ask: Which defect best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency raises chylomicrons and triglycerides, not **LDL 300 mg/dL**
whyNot.C: Apolipoprotein C-II deficiency raises chylomicrons, not **LDL 300 mg/dL**
whyNot.D: A transfer protein defect (abetalipoproteinemia) lowers LDL; his **LDL is 300 mg/dL**
whyNot.E: Apolipoprotein E2 raises remnants and gives palmar xanthomas, not **isolated LDL elevation**

why: Tendon xanthomas are cholesterol deposits in tendons seen in familial hypercholesterolemia from defective LDL receptors. **LDL 300 mg/dL with early family MI** confirms it.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Clenched fist held over the chest
Firm nodules on Achilles or knuckle tendons
Hypercholesterolemia if young; normal if old

idea.rule: Achilles tendon xanthomas with very high LDL = LDL receptor defect.
also: Corneal arcus under age 45 also suggests it

set_title: Lipid and coronary clues: Levine sign, Frank sign, Tendon xanthomas, Xanthelasma and Corneal arcus
stem: A 52-year-old woman has had 6 months of generalized itching and fatigue. Her alkaline phosphatase is elevated and antimitochondrial antibodies are positive. Soft yellow plaques are present on both upper eyelids.
oneliner: 52F, itching, high alkaline phosphatase, AMA positive + yellow plaques on eyelids → ?

whyNot.A: Levine sign is a clenched fist over the chest; hers are **yellow eyelid plaques**
whyNot.B: Frank sign is an earlobe crease; hers are **yellow plaques on the eyelids**
whyNot.C: Tendon xanthomas are on tendons; hers are **on the eyelids**
whyNot.E: Corneal arcus is a ring at the corneal edge; hers are **eyelid plaques**

why: Xanthelasma are yellow lipid plaques on the eyelids. In **primary biliary cholangitis**, cholestasis raises cholesterol, and these plaques are often present.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Clenched fist held over the chest
Firm nodules on Achilles or knuckle tendons
Hypercholesterolemia if young; normal if old

idea.rule: Yellow eyelid plaques = xanthelasma; check lipids and cholestasis.

set_title: Lipid and coronary clues: Levine sign, Frank sign, Tendon xanthomas, Xanthelasma and Corneal arcus
stem: A 30-year-old man has a gray-white ring at the periphery of both corneas. He has no other complaints.
oneliner: 30M + gray-white ring at the periphery of both corneas → ?

whyNot.A: Wilson disease gives a golden-brown Kayser-Fleischer ring, not a **gray-white** one
whyNot.B: Hypercalcemia causes band keratopathy across the central cornea, not a **peripheral ring**
whyNot.D: Marfan syndrome causes lens dislocation, not a **peripheral corneal ring**
whyNot.E: Vitamin A deficiency causes Bitot spots, not a **gray-white corneal ring**

why: Corneal arcus is lipid deposition at the corneal periphery. It is normal in the elderly but at **age 30** it suggests hypercholesterolemia.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Clenched fist held over the chest
Firm nodules on Achilles or knuckle tendons
Hypercholesterolemia if young; normal if old

idea.rule: Corneal arcus under age 45 = check for familial hypercholesterolemia.

set_title: Heart shapes on chest x-ray: Boot-shaped heart, Egg on a string, Snowman sign, Rib notching and Water-bottle heart
stem: A 2-year-old boy is cyanotic and squats after playing. A harsh systolic ejection murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border. Chest x-ray shows an upturned cardiac apex with a concave pulmonary segment.
oneliner: 2M, cyanosis, squats + upturned cardiac apex, concave pulmonary segment → ?

whyNot.A: Egg on a string is transposition's oval heart; his has an **upturned apex**
whyNot.B: Snowman sign is a figure-8 with wide upper mediastinum; his has an **upturned apex**
whyNot.C: Rib notching is scalloped ribs of coarctation; his film shows an **upturned apex**
whyNot.D: Water-bottle heart is globular enlargement; his silhouette has an **upturned apex**

why: Boot-shaped heart is an upturned apex from right ventricular hypertrophy with a small pulmonary trunk, seen in tetralogy of Fallot. **Squatting and cyanosis** fit.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Figure-8 heart with wide upper mediastinum
Supracardiac total anomalous pulmonary venous return

idea.rule: Upturned apex and concave pulmonary segment = tetralogy of Fallot.
also: Squatting raises systemic resistance, reducing shunt

set_title: Heart shapes on chest x-ray: Boot-shaped heart, Egg on a string, Snowman sign, Rib notching and Water-bottle heart
stem: A newborn boy becomes cyanotic within hours of birth, and the cyanosis does not improve with oxygen. Chest x-ray shows an oval cardiac silhouette with a narrow superior mediastinum.
oneliner: Newborn boy, cyanosis within hours + oval heart, narrow superior mediastinum → ?

whyNot.B: Boot-shaped heart has an upturned apex; this film shows an **oval heart, narrow mediastinum**
whyNot.C: Snowman sign has a wide upper mediastinum; his mediastinum is **narrow**
whyNot.D: Rib notching occurs in older children with coarctation; this is a **newborn**
whyNot.E: Water-bottle heart is globular enlargement; his mediastinum is **narrow** with an oval heart

why: Egg on a string is an oval heart on a narrow mediastinum, classic for transposition of the great arteries. **Early cyanosis not corrected by oxygen** fits the parallel circulations.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Figure-8 heart with wide upper mediastinum
Supracardiac total anomalous pulmonary venous return

idea.rule: Oval heart with narrow mediastinum in a cyanotic newborn = transposition.

set_title: Heart shapes on chest x-ray: Boot-shaped heart, Egg on a string, Snowman sign, Rib notching and Water-bottle heart
stem: A 3-month-old girl is cyanotic and tachypneic. Chest x-ray shows a figure-8 cardiac silhouette with a widened upper mediastinum.
oneliner: 3-month-old girl, cyanosis, tachypnea + figure-8 heart, wide upper mediastinum → ?
ask: Which anomaly best explains this sign?

options.A: Transposition of the great arteries with VSD
options.B: Tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary atresia

whyNot.A: Transposition shows an egg-shaped heart, not a **figure-8 with wide upper mediastinum**
whyNot.B: Tetralogy shows a boot-shaped heart, not a **figure-8 silhouette**
whyNot.C: Coarctation does not cause **cyanosis with a figure-8 silhouette**
whyNot.E: Tricuspid atresia gives left axis deviation and a small right heart, not a **figure-8**

why: Snowman sign is a figure-8 silhouette in supracardiac total anomalous pulmonary venous return, where a dilated vertical vein and superior vena cava widen the upper mediastinum. **Infant cyanosis** fits.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Figure-8 heart with wide upper mediastinum
Supracardiac total anomalous pulmonary venous return

idea.rule: Figure-8 heart with wide upper mediastinum = supracardiac TAPVR.
also: All pulmonary veins drain to the right atrium

set_title: Heart shapes on chest x-ray: Boot-shaped heart, Egg on a string, Snowman sign, Rib notching and Water-bottle heart
stem: A 15-year-old boy has headaches and BP 165/95 mm Hg in the right arm. Femoral pulses are weak and delayed. Chest x-ray shows scalloped inferior margins of the posterior ribs.
oneliner: 15M, arm hypertension, weak femoral pulses + scalloped inferior rib margins → ?
ask: Which process best explains this sign?

options.A: Neurofibromas arising from the intercostal nerves
options.B: Healed rib fractures from old trauma

whyNot.A: Neurofibromas can notch ribs but do not cause **weak femoral pulses with arm hypertension**
whyNot.B: Old fractures do not explain **weak femoral pulses with arm hypertension**
whyNot.C: Myeloma causes punched-out lesions, not **scalloped ribs with arm hypertension**
whyNot.D: Pleural plaques are calcified pleural opacities, not **scalloped inferior rib margins**

why: Rib notching is scalloping of the inferior posterior ribs from enlarged intercostal collaterals bypassing a coarctation. **Arm hypertension with weak femoral pulses** confirms it.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Figure-8 heart with wide upper mediastinum
Supracardiac total anomalous pulmonary venous return

idea.rule: Scalloped inferior ribs with arm hypertension = coarctation collaterals.

set_title: Chest and airway signs: Hamman crunch, Hoover sign, Platypnea-orthodeoxia, Oliver sign (tracheal tug) and Pemberton sign
stem: A 64-year-old man with hoarseness has a pulsatile chest mass. When his larynx is gently lifted upward, a downward tug of the trachea is felt with each heartbeat.
oneliner: 64M, hoarseness + trachea tugs downward with each heartbeat → ?
ask: Which vascular lesion best explains this sign?

whyNot.B: An abdominal aneurysm does not tug the trachea; he has **downward tracheal tug**
whyNot.C: Carotid stenosis causes bruits, not a **downward tracheal tug and hoarseness**
whyNot.D: Coarctation causes arm hypertension, not a **tracheal tug**
whyNot.E: Subclavian stenosis causes arm pressure differences, not a **tracheal tug**

why: Oliver sign is a downward tug of the trachea with each pulse, transmitted by an aneurysm of the aortic arch. **Hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve stretch** supports it.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Lower ribs pull inward on inspiration
Dyspnea and hypoxia when upright, better lying
Trachea tugs downward with each heartbeat
Face flushes when both arms are raised
Substernal goiter obstructing the thoracic inlet

idea.rule: Trachea tugs down with each pulse = aortic arch aneurysm.

set_title: Heat and cold triggered signs: Uhthoff phenomenon, Raynaud phenomenon, Ice pack test, Cold-induced acrocyanosis and Ice cube test
stem: A 42-year-old woman has tight skin over her fingers, heartburn and exertional dyspnea. In cold weather her fingers turn white, then blue, then red with throbbing pain on rewarming. Anti-centromere antibodies are positive.
oneliner: 42F, tight finger skin, heartburn + fingers white, blue, then red in the cold → ?

whyNot.A: Uhthoff is heat worsening neurologic deficits; hers is **cold-triggered colour change**
whyNot.C: The ice pack test relieves eyelid ptosis; hers is **finger colour change in cold**
whyNot.D: Acrocyanosis is persistent blueness; hers **cycles white, blue, then red**
whyNot.E: The ice cube test raises a local wheal; hers **cycles white, blue, then red**

why: Cold triggers digital artery vasospasm, giving pallor, cyanosis, then reactive redness. **Tight skin and anti-centromere antibodies** indicate secondary Raynaud from systemic sclerosis.

idea.rule: Fingers white, blue, red with cold = Raynaud; secondary suggests scleroderma.
also: Primary Raynaud: young woman, no disease

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Heat or exercise worsens neurologic symptoms
Fingers white, blue, then red with cold
Blue fingertips and ears in cold
Ice on skin raises a wheal

set_title: Fundus signs: Cherry-red spot, Hollenhorst plaque, Cotton-wool spots, AV nicking and Blood and thunder fundus
stem: A 66-year-old smoker has had 5 minutes of a curtain falling over the left eye that resolved fully. Funduscopy shows a bright yellow, refractile body lodged at a retinal arteriole bifurcation.
oneliner: 66M smoker, transient monocular blindness + bright yellow body in retinal arteriole → ?

whyNot.A: Cherry-red spot needs a pale retina and lasting blindness; his vision **recovered**
whyNot.B: Cotton-wool spots are fluffy white patches; he has a **bright refractile body**
whyNot.C: AV nicking is vein compression at crossings; he has a **lodged yellow body**
whyNot.D: Blood and thunder is diffuse hemorrhage; his retina shows a **single yellow body**

why: A bright yellow refractile body in a retinal arteriole is a Hollenhorst plaque, a cholesterol embolus from carotid atherosclerosis that caused amaurosis fugax.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Bright yellow plaque in retinal artery
Widespread hemorrhages, swollen veins, disc edema

idea.rule: Yellow refractile retinal body + amaurosis fugax = Hollenhorst; check the carotid.

set_title: Childhood rash clues: Koplik spots, Forchheimer spots, Pastia lines, Slapped cheeks and Strawberry tongue
stem: A 2-year-old boy has 6 days of fever at 39.5 C, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, swollen red hands and a bright red tongue with prominent papillae.
oneliner: 2M, 6 days fever + red eyes, swollen hands, red tongue with prominent papillae → ?
ask: Which vessels are at greatest risk from this disease?

whyNot.A: Renal aneurysms occur in polyarteritis nodosa; this toddler has **Kawasaki features**
whyNot.C: Berry aneurysms are not the complication of a toddler with **fever and red tongue**
whyNot.D: Pulmonary artery aneurysms occur in Behcet disease; he has **Kawasaki features**
whyNot.E: Mesenteric aneurysms occur in polyarteritis nodosa; he has **Kawasaki findings**

why: Fever over 5 days with conjunctivitis, hand swelling and strawberry tongue is Kawasaki disease. Medium-vessel vasculitis threatens the coronary arteries; treat with IVIG and aspirin.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Blue-white spots on red buccal mucosa
Red petechiae on the soft palate
Bright red cheeks, then lacy body rash

idea.rule: Strawberry tongue with 5+ days of fever = Kawasaki; coronary aneurysms.

set_title: Vascular bedside tests: Homans sign, Allen test, Adson test, Blue toe syndrome and Arm blood pressure difference
stem: A 66-year-old man has 3 days of painful purple discoloration of several digits of both feet, 2 days after femoral cardiac catheterization. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are strongly palpable. Creatinine rose from 1.2 to 2.4 mg/dL, and eosinophils are 9%.
oneliner: 66M, post-catheterization + painful purple foot digits + intact pulses + AKI → ?

whyNot.A: Homans sign is calf pain on dorsiflexion; he has **purple digits with strong pulses**
whyNot.B: Allen test checks hand perfusion; his findings are in the **feet**
whyNot.C: Adson test changes the radial pulse with neck turning; his **pedal pulses are intact**
whyNot.E: Arm pressure difference reflects subclavian stenosis, not **foot digit ischemia after catheterization**

why: Painful purple digits with **intact pulses** after arterial catheterization are blue toe syndrome: cholesterol emboli lodge in small distal arteries, also causing AKI and eosinophilia.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Palm stays pale after ulnar release
Inadequate ulnar collateral flow (radial puncture unsafe)
Radial pulse fades with neck turn, deep breath
Lower BP and weak pulse in one arm

idea.rule: Purple digits + intact pulses after catheterization = cholesterol emboli (blue toe syndrome).

set_title: Vascular bedside tests: Homans sign, Allen test, Adson test, Blue toe syndrome and Arm blood pressure difference
stem: A 41-year-old woman needs a radial artery blood gas. The examiner compresses both her radial and ulnar arteries while she clenches her fist, then she opens her pale hand. After the ulnar artery is released, the palm remains pale for 15 seconds.
oneliner: 41F, before radial blood gas + palm stays pale after ulnar release → ?

whyNot.B: Homans sign is calf pain on dorsiflexion; this exam involves **wrist compression**
whyNot.C: Adson test checks radial pulse with neck rotation; this exam **releases ulnar compression**
whyNot.D: Blue toe syndrome is embolic foot ischemia, not a **pale palm after ulnar release**
whyNot.E: That compares arm pressures; here the exam is **hand compression and release**

why: A palm that **stays pale after ulnar release** is an abnormal Allen test, meaning inadequate ulnar collateral flow; radial puncture is unsafe.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Palm stays pale after ulnar release
Inadequate ulnar collateral flow (radial puncture unsafe)
Radial pulse fades with neck turn, deep breath
Lower BP and weak pulse in one arm

idea.rule: Pale palm persisting after ulnar release = abnormal Allen test; avoid radial puncture.
also: Tests ulnar supply of the palmar arch

set_title: Vascular bedside tests: Homans sign, Allen test, Adson test, Blue toe syndrome and Arm blood pressure difference
stem: A 67-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history has episodes of lightheadedness and blurred vision when he paints ceilings with his left arm. Left brachial blood pressure is 95/60 mm Hg and right is 150/85 mm Hg. The left radial pulse is weak.
oneliner: 67M, smoker + dizziness with left arm use + left BP 95/60 vs right 150/85 → ?
ask: Which diagnosis best explains these findings?

options.A: Thoracic outlet syndrome from a cervical rib

whyNot.A: Thoracic outlet compression causes arm pain and paresthesia, not **dizziness with arm use**
whyNot.B: Coarctation presents earlier with rib notching; he is **67 with dizziness on arm use**
whyNot.C: Dissection causes sudden tearing pain, not **recurrent dizziness with arm exertion**
whyNot.E: Takayasu arteritis occurs in young women, not a **67-year-old smoker**

why: Lower pressure and a weak pulse in one arm with **dizziness during arm use** indicate subclavian steal: proximal stenosis reverses vertebral flow toward the arm.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Palm stays pale after ulnar release
Inadequate ulnar collateral flow (radial puncture unsafe)
Radial pulse fades with neck turn, deep breath
Lower BP and weak pulse in one arm

idea.rule: Arm BP difference + dizziness with arm exercise = subclavian steal (proximal stenosis).

set_title: Breathing patterns: Kussmaul, Cheyne-Stokes, Biot, apneustic and central neurogenic
stem: A 71-year-old man with heart failure (ejection fraction 20%) is watched overnight. His breathing slowly deepens, then grows shallower, then stops for 20 seconds before the cycle repeats. The nurse charts Cheyne-Stokes breathing.
oneliner: 71M, heart failure with EF 20% + Cheyne-Stokes breathing at night → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains this breathing pattern?

options.B: Loss of pontine signals that end inspiration
options.C: Damage to the medullary respiratory rhythm generator
options.D: Upper airway collapse during sleep despite effort
options.E: Delayed CO2 feedback from slow circulation

whyNot.A: That is Kussmaul breathing; his pattern **deepens, fades and pauses**
whyNot.B: That causes apneustic breathing; his breaths **slowly deepen and fade**, never held
whyNot.C: That causes chaotic Biot breathing; his cycle **repeats regularly**
whyNot.D: Obstructive apnea shows effort against a closed airway; his breathing **simply stops**

answer: Delayed CO2 feedback from slow circulation
why: Breaths crescendo, decrescendo, then pause. Slow blood flow in heart failure delays CO2 signals to the chemoreceptors, so breathing overshoots and then undershoots.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Breaths swell, fade, then pause; repeats
Irregular breaths and pauses, no pattern
Lower pons lesion, e.g. basilar stroke
Fast deep breaths without metabolic acidosis

idea.rule: Waxing-waning breaths with apneas in heart failure = Cheyne-Stokes from delayed feedback.
also: Also after bilateral cerebral hemisphere damage
Common during sleep at high altitude

set_title: Pulse signs: paradoxus, alternans, parvus et tardus, water-hammer and bisferiens
stem: A 48-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer has 2 days of worsening breathlessness. Pulse is 124/min and blood pressure 92/60 mm Hg. Neck veins are distended and heart sounds are muffled. Systolic pressure is 92 mm Hg on expiration and 76 mm Hg on inspiration.
oneliner: 48F, lung cancer + JVD, muffled heart sounds, systolic 92 → 76 on inspiration → ?

whyNot.A: Alternans varies beat to beat; her pressure falls **with each inspiration**
whyNot.B: Parvus et tardus is a weak, late upstroke; her pressure falls **only on inspiration**
whyNot.C: Water-hammer pulse bounds with a wide pulse pressure; hers is **92/60**
whyNot.E: Bisferiens has two peaks per beat; her systolic pressure **drops 16 mm Hg on inspiration**

why: A 16 mm Hg inspiratory systolic fall is pulsus paradoxus. Fluid fixes total heart volume, so inspiratory right heart filling bows the septum and cuts left ventricular output.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Inspiratory systolic BP drop over 10 mm Hg
Regular rhythm, strong and weak beats alternate
Weak carotid pulse that peaks late
Bounding pulse that rises and collapses fast
Two systolic peaks in each beat

idea.rule: Inspiratory systolic drop over 10 mm Hg + JVD + muffled sounds = tamponade.
also: Beck triad: hypotension, JVD, muffled sounds

set_title: Pulse signs: paradoxus, alternans, parvus et tardus, water-hammer and bisferiens
stem: A 76-year-old man has had dizziness and chest tightness while climbing stairs for 3 months. His carotid pulse is weak and rises slowly to a late peak (pulsus parvus et tardus). S2 is soft and single.
oneliner: 76M, exertional dizziness and chest tightness + pulsus parvus et tardus, soft single S2 → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Regurgitation gives a bounding, collapsing pulse, not a **weak, slow-rising** one
whyNot.C: Tamponade causes pulsus paradoxus; his finding is a **slow, late carotid peak**
whyNot.D: HCM gives a brisk, two-peaked pulse; his pulse is **weak and rises slowly**
whyNot.E: Dilated cardiomyopathy gives pulsus alternans; his clue is a **late peak with soft single S2**

why: A narrowed aortic valve slows left ventricular ejection, so the carotid pulse is small and late. Exertional angina, syncope and dyspnea follow the fixed outflow.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Inspiratory systolic BP drop over 10 mm Hg
Regular rhythm, strong and weak beats alternate
Weak carotid pulse that peaks late
Bounding pulse that rises and collapses fast
Two systolic peaks in each beat

idea.rule: Weak, late carotid pulse + soft single S2 in an older adult = aortic stenosis.
also: Crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids

set_title: Pulse signs: paradoxus, alternans, parvus et tardus, water-hammer and bisferiens
stem: A 34-year-old man with Marfan syndrome has tired easily for a year. Blood pressure is 164/42 mm Hg. When the examiner raises his arm and grips the forearm, the pulse strikes the fingers hard and then falls away abruptly. His head bobs with each heartbeat.
oneliner: 34M, Marfan + BP 164/42, hard pulse that falls away abruptly, head bobbing → ?

whyNot.A: Paradoxus is an inspiratory BP fall; his clue is **164/42 with a collapsing pulse**
whyNot.B: Alternans swaps strong and weak beats; **every beat strikes hard**
whyNot.C: Parvus et tardus is weak and slow; his pulse **strikes the fingers hard**
whyNot.D: Bisferiens is felt as two peaks; his pulse **falls away abruptly** after one

why: A hard, fast-rising pulse that collapses is the water-hammer (Corrigan) pulse. A large stroke volume raises systolic pressure; backflow into the ventricle drops diastolic pressure fast.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Inspiratory systolic BP drop over 10 mm Hg
Regular rhythm, strong and weak beats alternate
Weak carotid pulse that peaks late
Bounding pulse that rises and collapses fast
Two systolic peaks in each beat

idea.rule: Wide pulse pressure + bounding, collapsing pulse = chronic aortic regurgitation.

set_title: Pulse signs: paradoxus, alternans, parvus et tardus, water-hammer and bisferiens
stem: A 66-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy has worsening dyspnea. Ejection fraction is 15%. ECG shows regular sinus rhythm. The radial pulse shows pulsus alternans: strong and weak beats alternate.
oneliner: 66M, dilated cardiomyopathy, EF 15%, sinus rhythm + pulsus alternans → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains this sign?

options.B: Fluid restricting filling of all chambers
options.C: Fixed obstruction at the aortic valve
options.D: Large diastolic backflow across the aortic valve
options.E: Dynamic septal obstruction of LV outflow

whyNot.B: That is tamponade, giving pulsus paradoxus; he has **dilated cardiomyopathy, EF 15%**
whyNot.C: Aortic stenosis gives a slow, weak pulse; his beats **alternate strong and weak**
whyNot.D: Regurgitation bounds on every beat; his **strong and weak beats alternate**
whyNot.E: HCM obstruction gives a two-peaked pulse; his ventricle is **dilated with EF 15%**

why: In regular rhythm, alternating strong and weak beats mean a failing left ventricle whose contractile force swings from beat to beat.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Inspiratory systolic BP drop over 10 mm Hg
Regular rhythm, strong and weak beats alternate
Weak carotid pulse that peaks late
Bounding pulse that rises and collapses fast
Two systolic peaks in each beat

idea.rule: Alternating pulse strength in sinus rhythm = severe LV systolic dysfunction.
also: Poor prognostic sign in heart failure
